statement: The triangular numbers are $1, 3, 6, 10, 15, \ldots$, where the $n$th triangular number is $1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \dfrac{n(n + 1)}{2}$. How many of the first $100$ triangular numbers are odd?

choices.misconception: I thought that since n(n + 1) is always even, n(n + 1)/2 must be even too, but half of an even number can be odd.
I thought only one triangular number in every four is odd, but the pattern is odd, odd, even, even.
I thought the pattern was odd, odd, even, repeating every three, so I counted the n from 1 to 100 that are not multiples of 3.
I thought n(n + 1)/2 is even only when n is a multiple of 4, but it is also even when n + 1 is a multiple of 4.

hints: Write down whether each of the first eight triangular numbers is odd or even.
The pattern is odd, odd, even, even, and then it repeats every four.
$\dfrac{n(n + 1)}{2}$ is even exactly when $n$ or $n + 1$ is a multiple of $4$. So it is odd when $n$ leaves a remainder of $1$ or $2$ on division by $4$.

solutions.reliable: One of $n$ and $n + 1$ is even. If that even number is a multiple of $4$, then $\dfrac{n(n + 1)}{2}$ still has a factor of $2$ and is even. If the even number is $2$ times an odd number, halving it leaves a product of two odd numbers, which is odd. So the triangular number is odd exactly when $n$ leaves remainder $1$ or $2$ on division by $4$. Each block of four consecutive values of $n$ contains two of these, and $1$ to $100$ is $25$ full blocks, so $25 \cdot 2 = 50$ of the first $100$ triangular numbers are odd.
solutions.elegant: Each triangular number is the one before plus $n$. Adding an odd $n$ switches odd and even; adding an even $n$ keeps it. Starting from $1$ (odd), adding $2, 3, 4, 5, \ldots$ gives keep, switch, keep, switch, so the pattern is odd, odd, even, even, repeating every four. Half of the first $100$ are odd: $50$.
